items.title: After Oyo: Will Ambassadors Return?
items.description: Oyo got Mr Ruto and Mr Tshisekedi back in the same room.
content: The headline promise from Sunday’s four-party summit in Oyo, Republic of Congo, was the “return of ambassadors”. In Nairobi’s haste to claim a diplomatic victory, protocol is already running ahead of reality.

In Kinshasa, Kenyan political appointee Peter Tum, who had previously reported for duty despite being left in limbo without Congolese agrément , the host state’s formal diplomatic consent, has his X bio reading “Kenya’s Ambassador to the DRC”.
Under diplomatic protocol, however, an envoy remains a mere nominee until formal accreditation is granted and credentials are presented to the host president, making the title strictly aspirational.

President Tshisekedi’s administration is in no rush to play along. Asked whether the Congolese government will grant accreditation for the envoy, a senior official poured cold water on expectations of an instant reset.

“C’est un rapprochement graduel, les échanges vont se faire diplomatiquement. À ce stade on n’a pas de calendrier fixe pour cela,” the official said ( “It is a gradual rapprochement, the exchanges will be done diplomatically. At this point we don’t have a fixed schedule for this”.
Translated out of careful diplomatic French, the message is blunt: accreditation remains conditional, and Kinshasa refuses to be hurried by Nairobi’s domestic political calendar.
Having already stalled two consecutive Kenyan ambassadorial nominees, Congolese policymakers know withholding agrément is their sharpest lever.

With Kenya’s general election looming in August 2027, Mr Ruto urgently needs export growth, protection for over sh100 billion in Kenyan corporate investments, and momentum for the Mombasa-DRC trade corridor amid a global scramble for critical minerals.
Mr Tshisekedi faces no such immediate election clock, and Kinshasa will likely keep its agrément firmly on ice until Nairobi backs its words with action.

That caution explains why decoding the Oyo communiqué matters far more than celebrating the handshake. The summit produced predictable boilerplate like “mutual understanding,” “good-neighbourliness,” and “African solidarity.”

“I’d read it as a thaw, not a full reset yet,” says Bravin Onditi, a regional affairs analyst. “What they’ve agreed is just the basics: bring ambassadors back, revive the joint commission, and talk regularly.”

At its root, the breach between Nairobi and Kinshasa stems from a failure by Kenyan politicians under Mr Ruto to grasp the DRC’s strategic perspective, compounded by domestic political rivalries spilling into foreign policy.

Statecraft does not require agreeing with a neighbour’s worldview, only acknowledging its red lines. Worse, distrust has spilled beyond Kinshasa’s political elite into the Congolese public, where online commentators have urged caution toward Mr Ruto’s Oyo pledges.

This is a scepticism reinforced by Sudan’s military leadership accusing him last year of breaking a high-level promise not to back the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF), only for RSF figures to resurface in Nairobi shortly afterward to organise a parallel administration.
Placed side by side, the separate statements released by the Kenyan and Congolese presidencies hours after leaving Oyo read like accounts of two different meetings.

Mr Ruto’s statement stressed restoring ambassadorial ties, reviving the Joint Grand Commission for Cooperation, and deepening trade and regional integration. Crucially, it made zero mention of Rwanda, keeping Nairobi’s public posture strictly bilateral and neutral.

Tshisekedi’s readout told a sharper, more triumphant story for his domestic base. It led with solemn pledges on “state sovereignty, territorial integrity, [and] non-interference in internal affairs”, a diplomatic code for forcing Nairobi to rein in Congolese opposition figures, including Corneille Nangaa’s M23-allied Alliance Fleuve Congo (AFC) and allies of former president Joseph Kabila, who have used Nairobi to organise and address the press.
More tellingly, Kinshasa explicitly framed the summit as part of regional momentum against “Rwandan aggression”.

Each leader left Oyo with a tailored pitch. Mr Ruto sought to reassure anxious Kenyan boardrooms, from lenders like KCB and Equity to major retailers that their Congolese operations are safer. Mr Tshisekedi told Congolese voters he had compelled Nairobi to respect Congolese sovereignty.

Hours after the summit, a sharp public exchange on X laid bare just how raw those unresolved grievances remain. Responding to Mr Ruto’s post, former US Special Envoy for the Great Lakes J. Peter Pham warned that appeals to “solidarity and brotherhood” will ring hollow if Nairobi continues allowing M23 and eastern Congo armed groups to use Kenya as a de facto rear base, noting pointedly that no Kenyan rebels have ever held court at Kinshasa’s Fleuve Congo, Pullman, or Hilton hotels.

Kenya’s top foreign policy official, Korir Sing’oei, hit back furiously, dismissing critics as “manufacturers of innuendo” in faraway capitals who ignore the daily trade linking Goma and Nairobi, ending his rebuttal with a defiant “Washindwe!”
Yet by attacking the messenger rather than addressing the Nairobi hotel meetings directly, Nairobi inadvertently underscored why Kinshasa remains skeptical.

That divergence highlights the central contradiction of Oyo. Even though Rwanda’s role in eastern Congo sat at the very heart of the behind-the-scenes discussions and Kinshasa’s own readout blasted Rwandan aggression, Mr Ruto refused to sign onto any joint communiqué naming Kigali.

Nairobi’s calculation is obvious. Naming Rwanda in a joint text would blow up Ruto’s remaining channel with President Paul Kagame and destroy Kenya’s ties with Kigali. Yet by dodging the Rwanda question in public while Kinshasa spotlights it, Nairobi leaves the deepest root of mutual suspicion untouched.

It was, after all, Mr Ruto’s May 2024 remark in Kigali dismissing claims of Rwandan backing for M23 coming after Nairobi’s 2022 pivot from a promised offensive force to a passive buffer mandate that convinced Mr Tshisekedi to publicly accuse Ruto of siding with Rwanda at a Washington forum months later.
The Ebola Clause and a Missed Opportunity
Buried inside the Oyo communiqué is another revealing clue: a specific bullet point calling for bilateral cooperation “to eradicate the Ebola pandemic.”

In diplomacy, when a high-stakes political reconciliation text includes a routine public-health pledge, it means both sides needed a safe, non-controversial deliverable to show immediate goodwill while harder security compromises remain unfinished.

Yet that health clause also points to a smarter opportunity Nairobi missed months ago. Rather than waiting for third-party leaders in Congo-Brazzaville and Togo to broker a phone line, Kenya could have deployed health diplomacy on its own terms. Shipping a targeted package of medical supplies, diagnostic kits, and protective gear directly to Congolese doctors fighting Ebola (through Kinshasa) on the ground would have offered a credible, human-first reason to reopen direct contact without looking politically desperate.

Kenya’s scramble to reach Kinshasa via Brazzaville underscores a broader lesson in modern statecraft: allowing direct communication to collapse when relations turn rocky is almost always a strategic mistake.

History offers plenty of warnings. During the 1962 Cuban Missile Crisis, Washington and Moscow nearly stumbled into nuclear war partly because messages took hours to decode and deliver, prompting both superpowers to install the direct Moscow–Washington hotline so leaders could communicate via a direct teleprinter link precisely when distrust was highest.

More recently, after Beijing froze military talks with Washington over Taiwan in 2022, the resulting silence made the South China Sea far more dangerous. By late 2023, even as their rivalry deepened, the two superpowers had quietly reconnected their top brass and their presidents.
Closer to home, Nairobi’s own recent thaw with Sudan proved that diplomatic freezes quickly sour into mutual economic pain until self-interest forces both sides back to the table.

Talking to a rival, or an angry neighbour, is not a reward for good behaviour; it is basic risk management. When embassies sit empty and envoys go unaccredited, rumours replace intelligence, domestic politics harden, and a minor slight can spark a costly trade row.

Oyo got Mr Ruto and Mr Tshisekedi back in the same room. Turning a photo-op into a durable détente will mean keeping the line between Nairobi and Kinshasa open in foul weather and proving that Kenya’s word holds once the summit cameras leave.

Wetang’ula says CCTV showed MP pocketing colleague’s phone
items.description: Wetang’ula says he reviewed the footage with Kimani Ichung’wah and other MPs, but Citizen Digital does not identify the legislator or report any formal sanction.
content: Wetang’ula says he reviewed the footage with Kimani Ichung’wah and other MPs, but Citizen Digital does not identify the legislator or report any formal sanction.

Speaker Moses Wetang’ula says CCTV showed an MP pocketing another legislator’s phone, then denying it when confronted with the footage. He says he urged the member to reflect on the incident rather than describing a formal sanction.

Wetang’ula’s account, reported by Citizen Digital on November 25, 2026 , places the incident during a period of heightened tension in Parliament after a disagreement between members. The Speaker said CCTV footage was brought to his office and that he watched it with Majority Leader Kimani Ichung’wah and other MPs.

According to Wetang’ula, the footage showed one legislator putting another member’s phone in his pocket. The member was summoned and shown the video, the Speaker said, but denied taking the phone even while seeing himself in the footage. Citizen Digital quotes Wetang’ula saying, “We actually saw a member pocket the phone of another member.”

The report does not identify either legislator, say when the phone was taken, or describe what happened to the device afterwards. It also does not establish whether the member returned it. The account is therefore a public description by the Speaker, not a report identifying the person involved or detailing an independently examined recording.

Wetang’ula said he advised the MP to “wrestle with his conscience for the rest of this term,” adding that some conduct was not expected of members. He used the episode to urge MPs to behave honourably and protect the dignity of the House.

That is the response the report records. It does not say that the Speaker referred the matter to a parliamentary committee, opened a disciplinary process, or announced a penalty. Nor does it report a response from the unnamed MP. Without those details, it is not possible to tell whether the Speaker’s private rebuke was the only action taken or whether any further process followed.

The coverage also leaves the circumstances of the disagreement unclear. Wetang’ula linked the phone incident to a period when tensions were high, but Citizen Digital does not say what the members were arguing about or whether the disagreement involved the people connected to the phone. The account does not explain why the footage was brought to the Speaker, who first reported the phone missing, or whether other witnesses were consulted.

There is no second outlet’s account in the supplied coverage to compare with Citizen Digital’s report. That makes the Speaker’s description the sole account available here; it does not, by itself, show that the incident received little attention beyond the material provided. The central claim in the report is specifically attributed to Wetang’ula, who said he reviewed the CCTV with Ichung’wah and other MPs. The footage itself is not reproduced or independently described in the report.

The remaining questions are practical as well as political: who was involved, whether the phone was recovered, and whether Parliament took any formal action. The story, as reported, establishes what the Speaker says he saw and how he says he addressed the member. It does not answer those questions or confirm what followed.

Wetang’ula sends CCTV phone footage for committee review
items.description: Chege says the phone was hers; Wetang’ula has sent the footage to a committee that he says he will not chair.
content: Chege says the phone was hers; Wetang’ula has sent the footage to a committee that he says he will not chair.

National Assembly Speaker Moses Wetang’ula has referred CCTV footage of a colleague’s missing phone to the Powers and Privileges Committee after nominated MP Sabina Chege said the phone was hers and challenged him either to identify the person shown or have it returned. Wetang’ula will not chair the review, although he is the committee’s substantive chair.

The phone went missing during a confrontation in Parliament on June 8, 2023 , when Chege’s removal as Deputy Minority Whip was being contested. Chege told the House on Wednesday that she realised it was gone after Kisumu Town West MP Rozaah Buyu picked up her handbag during the commotion. She said she later tracked the phone from Parliament towards Donholm but never recovered it.

The accounts differ over what Wetang’ula said the footage showed. On Tuesday, he described seeing an MP pocket a colleague’s phone and said the legislator denied taking it when confronted with the recording. The Standard and The Star both carried that version. On Wednesday, after Chege identified herself as the owner, Wetang’ula said the footage showed a member picking up a phone from the seat where it had fallen. He maintained that he had said “taking”, not “stealing”.

Capital FM puts the shift in wording at the centre of the story: Wetang’ula had said he watched the recording with Majority Leader Kimani Ichung’wah and other MPs, but did not name the person. Tuko reports that his Wednesday wording referred to a male member . None of the reports identifies the MP, and the footage has not been made public in the accounts provided.

Wetang’ula said he would appoint another member to lead the committee’s review and bring a report to the House. The review is meant to establish what the footage shows; whether it can identify the person remains open. The reports give no date for the committee’s work or its report.

Mumias East MP Peter Salasya objected to the way the matter had become public, not simply to the allegation itself. Tuko and People Daily quote him warning that disclosures about internal disputes risk damaging Parliament’s reputation and turning embarrassing incidents into public entertainment. Salasya said the incident could be genuine while questioning whether a public disclosure was the right way to handle it.

The coverage also carries different details about the 2023 disorder. Tuko says seven MPs were suspended and Chege remained in her position after a court order. Capital FM recounts Chege’s account that she was caught up in a row involving Suba South MP Millie Odhiambo and Buyu. Tuko’s account of Wednesday’s exchange instead identifies Odhiambo as the MP who dismissed Chege’s concerns, and describes the original incident as involving Suba North MP Millie Odhiambo. The reports therefore differ on Odhiambo’s constituency; they do not explain the discrepancy.

The Star and People Daily add a separate episode that prompted Wetang’ula’s original remarks. Embakasi West MP Mark Mwenje asked him to review CCTV after social media claims that Mwenje had played video games during a sitting. Wetang’ula said he believed Mwenje was not responsible. The Star gives more detail about Mwenje’s concern that the allegation had reached his family and children. The reports do not establish who was playing the game.

What is now clear is that Chege has publicly claimed the missing phone and asked for an answer, while the Speaker has put the footage on a committee’s agenda. The MP’s identity, the phone’s whereabouts and the committee’s findings are still unresolved.
The Powers and Privileges Committee is to review the CCTV footage and report to the House.
The review may clarify what the footage shows and whether the person who picked up the phone can be identified.

items.title: Kenya will not relent on its bid to ensure clinker self-sufficiency for cement production – Ruto
items.description: President William Ruto has confirmed that the country will not back down from its commitment to ensure domestic clinker self-sufficiency by locally manufacturing the principal cement-making ingredient.
content: …as domestic cement consumption exceeded one million tonnes in a single month for the first time in July

President William Ruto has confirmed that the country will not back down from its commitment to ensure domestic clinker self-sufficiency by locally manufacturing the principal cement-making ingredient.

Speaking at a groundbreaking ceremony for the new US$250 million (KSh 32 billion) Bamburi Cement Plc Clinker Plant in Matuga, Kwale County, President Ruto dismissed sceptics, saying the national objective is to produce more of what we consume and retain more value within our economy.

He noted that clinker, the principal ingredient in cement, accounts for a high share of cement production costs. “When we import what we can competitively produce at home, we surrender opportunities to create jobs, develop skills and build industrial capacity. By producing clinker locally, we strengthen our manufacturers, preserve foreign exchange and create wealth in Kenya,” President Ruto stressed.

While commending Pan-African Business Conglomerate Amsons Group, led by Group Managing Director Mr Edha Nahdi, for the US$250 million investment, President Ruto noted that the investment comes at a time of strong growth in our construction industry. In 2025, the sector expanded by 6.8%, he said, while cement production increased by 18%, from 8.85 million tonnes in 2024 to 10.44 million tonnes in 2025.

Said President Ruto, “Our ambition must also extend beyond this market. In 2025, Kenya exported 2.21 million tonnes of clinker, up from million tonnes in 2024, to Uganda and Rwanda. We must improve our competitiveness, reduce transport costs, ensure fair access to clinker and make Kenyan cement a preferred choice at home and across the region.”

By doubling its clinker and cement production, Bamburi Cement, a member of the Amsons Group, will significantly contribute to President Ruto’s 10-year national development roadmap. The bold and ambitious KSh 5 trillion roadmap will be financed by the National Infrastructure Fund (NIF), which aims to transform Kenya into a first-world economy by developing and expanding strategic infrastructure such as roads, rail, ports, airports, and oil pipeline infrastructure that rely heavily on quality cement and concrete products.
In the first eight months of 2026, cement production grew by 14% to 7.62 million tonnes, up from 6.68 million tonnes produced last year, as domestic consumption exceeded one million tonnes in July.

President Ruto noted that, once complete, the plant will produce 5,000 tonnes of clinker daily, or about 1.6 million tonnes annually. The plant near Ngombeni will also increase Bamburi’s clinker production capacity from about one million to 2.6 million tonnes a year, and its cement production capacity from 1.8 million to four million tonnes.
“For families building homes, contractors constructing schools and counties developing roads, a reliable supply of quality cement at competitive prices is essential,” he noted.

He added, “Our Affordable Housing Programme demonstrates how these opportunities reinforce one another. Across all 47 counties, more than 313,000 homes are at various stages of construction, with some already completed, and the programme has generated over 1.1 million job opportunities.”

Through the turnkey clinkerisation plant, Kwale County, he said, has now taken its place on Kenya’s industrial map, joining West Pokot and Kitui in our national drive to turn our mineral resources into productive industries, create jobs, and expand economic opportunities across the country.

Speaking at the groundbreaking ceremony, Amsons Group Managing Director Mr Edha Nahdi reiterated that the new Matuga clinker plant, with best-in-class features including a 6-stage precalciner system, represents one of the firm’s most significant industrial investments through Bamburi Cement in recent years.

“For Amsons Group and Bamburi Cement, this US$ 250 million investment is a statement of our long-term confidence in Kenya and its economic potential. It is also part of our commitment to advance the value of local manufacturing as the engine of East Africa’s economic growth,” said Mr Nahdi.
The plant aligns Bamburi’s production with Amsons Group’s regional growth strategy, strengthening cross-border collaboration, supply-chain efficiency and market resilience across East Africa.

Bamburi Cement CEO Eng. Geoffrey Ndugwa, speaking at the ceremony, attended by Kwale County Governor H.E. Fatuma Mohamed Achani and Bamburi Cement Board Chairman Dr John Simba, among other dignitaries, said the clinkerisation plant construction works will be undertaken by Sinoma CBMI Construction Co., Ltd, one of the leading globally recognised engineering and construction firms in the cement industry.

“Clinker is the core ingredient at the heart of cement manufacturing, and policymakers have been exploring avenues to guarantee domestic self-sufficiency. With this groundbreaking, the new Bamburi Matuga Clinker Plant brings that heart home. This clinkerisation plant will shield Kenyan manufacturers from global supply shocks and currency swings, while lowering the cost of building in Kenya,” said Eng. Ndugwa.
By reducing reliance on imported clinker, the plant will save foreign exchange, help stabilise cement prices and secure supply for the domestic market.

As construction begins on the new Bamburi Matuga Clinker Plant, communities in Kwale and the wider coastal region also stand to benefit from over 10,000 direct and indirect jobs. Beyond jobs, the project will create opportunities for micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs) and local businesses in logistics, quarrying, equipment maintenance and other services across the region.
The project will also facilitate skills transfer, giving local people industrial experience that will remain at the Coast long after construction is complete.
Sinoma CBMI Construction Co., Ltd., part of the world-leading China National Building Material Group (CNBM), brings extensive expertise in cement plant engineering, procurement, and construction.

items.title: Ruto, Steinmeier agree to streamline jobs, visa processes for Kenyans
items.description: Kenya and Germany are seeking to expand employment opportunities for Kenyans in Germany, with the two countries agreeing to streamline visa and recruitment procedures and improve recognition of professional qualifications.
content: Kenya and Germany are seeking to expand employment opportunities for Kenyans in Germany, with the two countries agreeing to streamline visa and recruitment procedures and improve recognition of professional qualifications.

The move follows talks between President William Ruto and his German counterpart Frank-Walter Steinmeier at State House, Nairobi, where the two leaders witnessed the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) between Kenya and German language examination and certification institution telc.
The agreement is expected to ease access to internationally recognised German language certification, a key requirement for Kenyans seeking employment opportunities in Germany.
Ruto said the number of Kenyans employed in Germany had risen from 7,170 in March 2024 to 9,500 in March 2026, reflecting progress in the two countries’ overseas employment partnership.

“To build on this progress, we discussed measures to streamline visa and recruitment procedures, facilitate language training and accelerate the recognition of professional qualifications,” Ruto said.

The two leaders also discussed expanding economic cooperation, with Kenya welcoming Germany’s commitment of 52.5 million euros (approximately KSh7.8 billion) in development cooperation funding for the 2026-2028 period.

Ruto called for increased German investment in manufacturing, agro-processing, infrastructure, healthcare, renewable energy and digital technology, saying stronger economic ties should translate into tangible benefits for citizens.

Later, the two presidents attended a business roundtable bringing together Kenyan and German business delegations, where Ruto proposed the establishment of a Kenya-Germany Business Forum to strengthen trade and investment between the two countries.

He said Kenya’s strategic position as a gateway to the African market, coupled with the continent’s growing youthful population and expanding consumer market, presented opportunities for German businesses.

“As Africa moves from loans to investments, we are keen to unlock the continent’s vast economic potential through partnerships that create jobs, drive innovation and generate shared prosperity,” he said.
Ruto invited German investors to explore opportunities in energy, pharmaceuticals, agriculture, manufacturing and services.

items.title: MSEA advances grassroots industrialisation through common user machines
items.description: The Kariobangi Centre of Excellence, MSEA's model manufacturing and incubation hub, continues to advance grassroots enterprise development through access to productive infrastructure.
content: The Kariobangi Centre of Excellence, MSEA’s model manufacturing and incubation hub, continues to advance grassroots enterprise development through access to productive infrastructure. Today, the Centre hosted an economic empowerment forum during which 44 registered youth and women groups from Mathare Constituency received Common User Machines to strengthen their enterprise operations and productivity.

The forum was presided over by the Principal Secretary, State Department for MSMEs, Hon. Susan Auma Mang’eni, alongside Mathare Constituency MP, Hon. Tom Aluoch, MSEA Board Chairman, Dr. James Mureu, Board Members and Director General/CEO, Mr. Henry Rithaa, bringing together over 600 Micro and Small Enterprises (MSEs), including members of registered groups and associations.

In her address, the PS underscored the critical role of MSEs in Kenya’s economy, noting that they account for approximately 98% of businesses in the country. She highlighted the Government’s commitment to expanding economic opportunities for youth through programmes such as the National Youth Opportunities Towards Advancement (NYOTA), whose second phase is expected to extend support to more young entrepreneurse across the country.

She also encouraged MSEs to leverage the Kenya Jobs and Economic Transformation (KJET) Project, which strengthens MSME clusters through capacity building and co-investment support along priority value chains. Additionally, she sensitised participants on the ongoing AGPO training programme, accessible through *254#, which equips participants with the knowledge and certification needed to access government procurement opportunities. She urged youth and women to take advantage of the programme and explore available financing opportunities through the Hustler Fund, Uwezo Fund, Women Enterprise Fund and Youth Enterprise Development Fund.

Speaking during the forum, MSEA Director General/CEO, Mr. Henry Rithaa, encouraged the beneficiary groups to make productive use of the equipment, noting that access to appropriate machinery is essential in strengthening enterprise capacity, improving productivity and creating employment opportunities. He further emphasised the importance of organised groups in leveraging shared infrastructure to grow sustainable businesses.

The 44 beneficiary groups received a range of equipment, including car wash machines, welding machines, sewing machines, generators and woodworking machines. The equipment will support various enterprise activities, enhance production capabilities and open up additional income-generating opportunities for youth and women within Mathare Constituency.

Through Centres of Excellence and enterprise development programmes, MSEA continues to bring productive infrastructure, business support and economic opportunities closer to MSEs, advancing inclusive growth, job creation and the development of a competitive MSE sector.
Present at the forum were representatives from Uwezo Fund, Women Enterprise Fund, the National Government Administration and other stakeholders.

More than 10,000 jobs, new business opportunities: What the KSh32 billion Bamburi clinker plant in Kwale will bring
items.description: President William Ruto has launched a Sh32 billion clinker manufacturing plant in Matuga, Kwale County, in a major industrial investment expected to boost cement production, create thousands of jobs and strengthen Kenya’s manufacturing sector.
content: President William Ruto has launched a Sh32 billion clinker manufacturing plant in Matuga, Kwale County, in a major industrial investment expected to boost cement production, create thousands of jobs and strengthen Kenya’s manufacturing sector.

The groundbreaking ceremony, held on November 24, 2026, marks the start of a Sh32 billion (US$250 million) project by Bamburi Cement Plc, a member of Amsons Group, expected to significantly expand the country’s clinker production capacity and reduce reliance on imported raw materials.

The project, which is expected to generate more than 10,000 direct and indirect jobs, is also projected to unlock business opportunities for local entrepreneurs, transporters, suppliers and other enterprises across the Coast region.
President Ruto said the investment was a demonstration of the government’s commitment to strengthening local manufacturing, attracting capital and creating employment opportunities for Kenyans.

“Investments of this scale are important in building our manufacturing capacity, creating jobs for our young people and strengthening our economy. We want Kenya to increasingly produce locally what we consume and reduce our dependence on imports,” he said.
He said industrial investments should also translate into tangible benefits for communities, particularly through employment, business opportunities and improved livelihoods.

The plant will have an annual clinker production capacity of 1.6 million tonnes, with Bamburi Cement expected to increase its clinker output from approximately one million tonnes to 2.6 million tonnes annually.

The expansion will also raise the company’s cement production capacity from 1.8 million tonnes to four million tonnes per year, positioning it to meet growing demand driven by infrastructure development, housing and construction projects.

Clinker, a key ingredient in cement manufacturing, is partly sourced from imports, exposing manufacturers to fluctuations in global prices, foreign exchange pressures and disruptions in international supply chains.
The new facility is expected to strengthen local production, improve supply stability and support the government’s industrialisation agenda.

Beyond employment, the project is expected to create opportunities for small and medium-sized enterprises operating in transportation, logistics, construction supplies, equipment maintenance, quarrying and other supporting services.
Local businesses are expected to benefit from increased demand for goods and services as construction progresses and the plant begins operations.

The project will also provide opportunities for skills development and technology transfer, with workers expected to gain technical expertise and industrial experience that could support future manufacturing investments in the region.
For entrepreneurs in Kwale and neighbouring counties, the investment presents an opportunity to integrate into the supply chain of a major industrial facility.
The plant is expected to incorporate modern technologies aimed at improving energy efficiency and reducing its environmental footprint.
Bamburi plans to use Alternative Fuels and Raw Materials (AFR), including coconut husks, cashew nut husks and municipal solid waste sourced from the Coast, as part of its energy mix.
The initiative is expected to create additional opportunities for farmers, waste collectors, recycling enterprises and other players in the circular economy.

The use of agricultural residues and suitable waste materials in industrial production is also expected to support efforts to reduce reliance on conventional fuels while promoting sustainable manufacturing practices.
Amsons Group Managing Director Edha Nahdi said the investment reflected the group’s confidence in Kenya’s economic prospects and its commitment to supporting industrial development.

“Investing in a project of this magnitude reflects our confidence in Kenya and its economic potential. We believe local manufacturing is key to economic growth, job creation and building a more resilient industrial sector,” he said.
Nahdi said the project would strengthen local manufacturing capacity while contributing to economic growth and employment creation across the region.
Construction of the facility will be undertaken by Sinoma CBMI Construction Co. Ltd, an engineering firm specialising in cement plant construction.
The plant will incorporate a six-stage precalciner system, a modern technology designed to improve production efficiency.
Bamburi Cement has also outlined plans to support communities affected by the project through its Mwachome Village relocation programme, backed by Sh250 million.
The company said 112 project-affected persons from 42 households had undergone financial literacy training ahead of the second phase of compensation.
Bamburi Cement Board Chairman Dr John Simba said the investment must deliver benefits to surrounding communities alongside its industrial and economic objectives.

“The success of this project will not only be measured by the production capacity of the plant, but also by the positive impact it has on the communities around us. Their welfare, inclusion and participation in the opportunities created by this investment remain important,” he said.
Kwale Governor Fatuma Achani attended the ceremony alongside other national and county leaders.
The project comes as the government pursues a Sh5 trillion, 10-year development roadmap anchored on infrastructure expansion, industrialisation and economic transformation.
For Kwale County and the wider Coast region, the investment is expected to strengthen the industrial base while creating employment and opening new avenues for local businesses.

items.title: Sports Department Warns Sh8.38 Billion Budget Shortfall Could Jeopardise AFCON 2027 Preparations
items.description: Kenya's AFCON 2027 preparations face a potential funding challenge after the Sports Department disclosed an Sh8.38 billion recurrent budget shortfall.
content: State Department for Sports says it needs Sh10.78 billion in recurrent funding but has received only Sh2.39 billion as Kenya prepares for major international sporting competitions.
Newsroom · lets crawlers and assistive tech read the precise publication time while readers see a stable date with the year. --> 25 November 2026 · 3 min read

Kenya’s preparations to host the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) and the 2028 World Athletics Championships could face financial challenges after the State Department for Sports revealed an Sh8.38 billion funding shortfall in its proposed 2027/2028 budget.
Principal Secretary Elijah Mwangi raised the concern before the National Assembly Sports and Culture Committee, chaired by Dan Wanyama, while presenting the department’s budget proposals.

Mwangi said the department requires Sh10.78 billion to meet its recurrent expenditure obligations in the 2027/2028 financial year but has been allocated only Sh2.39 billion under the Budget Policy Statement (BPS).
The allocation leaves a deficit of Sh8.38 billion, which the PS warned could undermine the department’s ability to implement critical programmes and meet its financial obligations.
Mwangi attributed the increased budgetary requirements partly to preparations for hosting major international sporting competitions.
According to the PS, AFCON 2027 preparations require Sh3.55 billion, while preparations for the 2029 World Athletics Championships require approximately Sh3.9 billion.
He told MPs that the proposed funding would also cater for essential recurrent expenses needed to sustain departmental operations and deliver its core programmes.
“The higher requirement in FY 2027/28 are for preparation to host AFCON 2027 which is Sh3,546,789,165 and the 2029 World Athletics Championships which is Sh3.9 billion,” Mwangi told the committee.

The department's total resource requirement for the 2027/2028 financial year stands at Sh42.01 billion, comprising Sh10.78 billion for recurrent expenditure and Sh31.23 billion for development programmes.
However, the Budget Policy Statement provides an allocation of Sh27.75 billion, leaving the department with an overall funding gap of approximately Sh14.26 billion.

The shortfall raises questions about the government's financial preparedness to deliver the infrastructure, logistics and administrative requirements associated with hosting major international sporting events.

During the committee proceedings, Wanyama urged the department to ensure that available resources are fairly distributed, particularly in settling outstanding debts owed to sports federations and other creditors.
He also called for the completion of sports academies being established across constituencies, noting the importance of investing in grassroots talent development.

The committee chairperson observed that funding national teams remained one of the primary responsibilities of the Sports Fund but expressed concern over the financial difficulties facing several federations.

“The issue of funding of national team was one of the priority things that the sports fund must do. So far we are doing well but federations have issues that you have quite a number of debts to pay to them and they are having a lot of problems,” Wanyama said.

Meanwhile, the State Department for Youth Affairs and Creative Economy, led by Principal Secretary Jacob Fikirini, raised concerns over the lack of funding for film location mapping in the 2027/2028 financial year.
Fikirini told MPs that the project remained ongoing and was expected to be completed by June 2027.

The department further reported receiving a recurrent allocation of Sh974.95 million in the current financial year, against expenditure of Sh400.99 million, representing an absorption rate of 41 percent.

Separately, Principal Secretary Ummi Bashir of the State Department for Culture, Arts and Heritage asked the committee to recommend additional funding to support departmental programmes and responsibilities.

The department cited inadequate funding for key priorities among its semi-autonomous government agencies, including the National Lottery Board, Kenya National Library Service and National Heroes Council.
It said additional resources were necessary to enable the institutions to implement planned activities and fulfil their respective mandates.

The Lagos visit was not purely personal. Majors also took part in the second edition of the AFRIFF Film and Content Market (AFCM), a platform where filmmakers, investors and entertainment industry leaders came together to discuss financing African productions and expanding their global reach.

Representatives from MBO Capital, Logical Pictures Group, Filmhouse Group and several other organisations involved in production and distribution were among those present for the roundtable discussions.
Majors described the experience as transformative, saying it reconnected him with the reason he pursued acting in the first place.
He also expressed a clear desire to be part of building that future.

Other industry leaders also highlighted challenges facing African cinema, particularly funding, infrastructure and technical expertise.
Adekunle Adebiyi, Executive Director of Investments at MBO Capital, argued that African filmmakers needed more locally sourced financing to maintain control over their stories.
He warned that relying heavily on foreign funding could influence the narratives eventually told on screen.
Frédéric Fiore, CEO of Logical Pictures Group, stressed that African film productions needed to generate commercial returns to attract investors.
He also highlighted gaps in post-production facilities, citing a Senegalese production that had to complete its post-production work in France.

Meanwhile, Joël Chikapa-Phiri of Known Associates Group called for greater investment in technical skills, questioning whether the continent had enough trained colour graders and visual effects professionals to support its growing film industry.
AFRIFF founder Chioma Ude also emphasised the need for strong African institutions, investment and infrastructure to help locally produced stories compete internationally.

The investment discussions included MBO Capital, Logical Pictures Group, Filmhouse Group and other financial and entertainment organisations.
Participating creative businesses were seeking between $250,000 and $5 million in funding.

Although Majors did not announce a specific African film project or financial investment, his participation highlighted his interest in connecting with filmmakers on the continent and supporting African storytelling.

content: The Future Isn’t Being Imported. It’s Being Built Here.

For too long, the narrative around African innovation has been about leapfrogging with "lite" versions of Western apps. But Nairobi is no longer just the "Silicon Savannah", it is rapidly evolving into a global testbed for frontier technologies. The era of the simple "Uber for X" is over. The next wave of valuation, the next generation of unicorns, will be driven by Deep Tech: proprietary, hard-to-replicate science and engineering that solves systemic problems at scale.

Startup Grind Nairobi Week will take place from November 23 to 27, 2026, bringing together deep tech founders, investors, engineers and regulators to explore Africa's emerging frontier technology ecosystem.

A massive gap exists in the ecosystem. Deep Tech founders, those building in AI, Blockchain, and Hardware, struggle to communicate their complex value propositions to generalist investors. Meanwhile, regulators are racing to keep pace with the rapid adoption of Crypto and AI, and users are desperate for solutions that actually understand their context.

items.description: The findings raise concerns about how businesses handle sensitive customer and company information as AI becomes increasingly integrated into everyday applications and business processes.
content: NAIROBI, Kenya Nov 25 – Kenyan businesses could be exposing themselves to data privacy and security risks through artificial intelligence tools already embedded in their operations, with a new report warning that most organisations lack basic safeguards to manage the technology.

The AI Readiness in Kenya 2026 report by the Kenya National Chamber of Commerce and Industry (KNCCI) and Akili AI reveals that four in five organisations using AI have no designated official responsible for overseeing risks associated with the technology.
The assessment further shows that three-quarters of organisations have no formal AI policy, while seven in ten lack the capacity to detect or respond to AI-related incidents.
The findings raise concerns about how businesses handle sensitive customer and company information as AI becomes increasingly integrated into everyday applications and business processes.

According to the report, many organisations are unaware of the extent to which AI is already being used within their operations, with employees independently adopting publicly available tools without clear internal guidelines.

Uasin Gishu youth agri-preneurs embrace technology to transform smallholder farming
items.description: Uasin Gishu youth agri-preneurs embrace technology to transform smallholder farming Kenya News Agency
content: More than 100 young agricultural entrepreneurs in Uasin Gishu County are being equipped with modern farming technologies, innovations and management practices in an initiative aimed at transforming smallholder agriculture, closing extension service gaps and strengthening food security.

The youth, trained under the National Agricultural Value Chain Development Project (NAVCDP), are expected to become a critical link between farmers and agricultural service providers by taking modern farming knowledge and solutions to the grassroots.

With one agri-preneurs deployed in each of the county’s 110 sub-locations, the initiative seeks to ensure farmers, particularly those in remote areas, have easier access to agricultural information, quality farm inputs, mechanization services, financial products and reliable markets.

The five-day training, which brought together the agri-preneurs, focused on technologies, innovations and improved field management practices across five priority value chains: coffee, avocado, dairy, potatoes and poultry.

County NAVCDP Project Coordinator Cosmas Langat said the programme was designed not only to improve agricultural productivity but also to empower young people to establish sustainable enterprises while providing essential services to farmers.

Langat noted that the agri-preneurs model, which has been rolled out nationally over the past year, was gaining momentum, with Uasin Gishu deploying 110 trained youth to serve farmers across all its sub-locations.

“We want, apart from extending agricultural technologies to farmers, to also impart the agri-preneurs with knowledge and skills that will enable them to link farmers with input suppliers, markets and other service providers while earning from the programme,” he said.

He explained that the initiative was intended to move farmers beyond subsistence production by exposing them to improved farming methods and commercial opportunities that could increase household incomes.

According to Langat, the youth would play a significant role in identifying farmers’ needs, providing technical guidance and facilitating connections with various players in the agricultural value chain.
The programme also presents an opportunity for young people to tap into agribusiness as a source of employment and income rather than viewing agriculture solely as a traditional farming activity.

Francis Ndegwa, who supports data and digital agriculture under NAVCDP, said the training was part of a broader capacity-building programme designed to equip the agri-preneurs with practical knowledge that they would subsequently pass on to farmers.
Ndegwa said the trained teams were expected to cascade the knowledge to the next level of agri-preneurs, who would then engage farmers across the five supported value chains.
He expressed optimism that the adoption of the technologies and recommended practices would translate into improved farm management, increased production, higher incomes and enhanced food security.

The training also seeks to strengthen the delivery of agricultural extension services at a time when government capacity to employ and deploy sufficient extension personnel has become increasingly constrained.
Ndegwa observed that agri-preneurs were emerging as an alternative channel for reaching farmers with timely technical information and practical solutions.
“Extension services have gone down, and that is why agri-preneurs are coming in to fill that gap,” he said.
Beyond offering technical advice, the youth are expected to establish linkages between farmers and providers of agricultural inputs, mechanization, markets, financing and insurance services.

Through these partnerships, farmers will be able to access essential services more conveniently, while the agri-preneurs will generate income through commissions and other business opportunities arising from the services they facilitate.

The model is also expected to promote digital agriculture through farmer registration, profiling, data collection and the use of digital advisory platforms to improve decision-making at the farm level.

By connecting smallholder farmers to input suppliers, financial institutions, SACCOs, aggregators and produce off-takers, the agri-preneurs will help strengthen the entire agricultural value chain and create opportunities for more organised commercial farming.

The initiative comes at a time when the agricultural sector continues to face challenges including limited access to extension services, rising production costs, climate-related risks and difficulties in accessing reliable markets.

Uasin Gishu County Director of Agriculture and Agribusiness, Reuben Seroney challenged the agri-preneurs to take advantage of the knowledge and skills acquired during the training to reach as many farmers as possible and help transform agricultural production.

Seroney urged the youth to be proactive in translating the training into practical interventions at the grassroots, noting that their role would be critical in supporting farmers to adopt modern farming technologies and improve productivity.

He said strengthening agricultural production and food security remained a key priority under the Bottom-Up Economic Transformation Agenda (BETA), which identifies agriculture as one of its key pillars.

Seroney encouraged the agri-preneurs to embrace their responsibility as frontline agricultural service providers by ensuring farmers benefit from the innovations, technologies and management practices introduced through the programme.

Through the deployment of youth agri-preneurs, NAVCDP seeks to address some of these challenges while creating a new generation of agricultural service providers capable of sustaining their businesses through the services they offer.

For Uasin Gishu, a county whose economy is largely anchored on agriculture, the success of the programme could have far-reaching implications for both rural livelihoods and the wider food production system.

With 110 agri-preneurs serving as the project’s grassroots link, the expectation is that improved farming knowledge, technology adoption and stronger market linkages will help farmers produce more, earn better returns and contribute to the country’s food security.

content: Meta has announced a $700,000 AI Impact Grant and a new AI Impact Hub for Africa, the Middle East and Turkiye. The announcement came at the AMET AI and Wearables Summit in Istanbul, held on 24 and 25 November under the theme “AI for Everyone.” Seven countries are eligible: Egypt, Kenya, Nigeria, Saudi Arabia, South Africa, Turkiye and the UAE.

The grant is aimed at startups and developers building on Meta’s AI tools and wearables, though it isn’t due to launch until 2027. The hub itself offers three learning tracks, an AI academy, general AI literacy training, and a small business track, with a stated goal of reaching more than five million people across the region over three years.
Kojo Boakye, Meta’s vice president of public policy for the region, said the aim is to help local innovators build AI products for their own problems rather than simply adopt tools built elsewhere.

Meta reported $64.6 billion in revenue for the third quarter of 2026 alone. At that run rate, the company earns roughly $8,100 every second. A $700,000 grant, spread across seven countries and meant to last through 2027, works out to about a minute and a half of Meta’s quarterly revenue.

That same quarter, Meta booked a $9.89 billion charge tied to an August settlement with 52 US state attorneys general. The contrast is simple arithmetic. A legal bill in the United States costs roughly fourteen thousand times more than the entire AI grant Meta is offering seven countries across Africa, the Middle East and Turkiye combined.
Innovators in the region should help shape AI’s future, not just adopt what’s built elsewhere.

Innovation Village reported in 2025 on Meta’s Llama Impact Accelerator, a six-week program that drew over 1,400 applications and picked 40 startups across Nigeria, Kenya, Senegal and South Africa, with twelve winners sharing just $200,000. First place in each country received $25,000.

A separate, larger Meta program the year before offered up to $2 million globally, with up to $500,000 per recipient, but that money was open to organisations in 90-plus countries worldwide, not ring-fenced for Africa. Measured against any of these, this week’s $700,000 for seven countries is a modest step up in headline size, not a changed order of magnitude.

Kenya is one of the seven countries this new grant targets, and it is also where Meta’s African troubles currently run deepest. Innovation Village reported in March that a Kenyan digital rights group petitioned the country’s data protection regulator over whether footage from Ray-Ban Meta glasses was used without authorisation to train Meta’s AI systems, after contractors reviewing that footage said they’d seen bathroom visits and bank card details.

More than eight months on, no public findings have been released. A separate, older case allows Kenyan content moderators to pursue a $1.6 billion claim against Meta and its outsourcing partner Sama through Kenya’s courts, years after it was first filed. Neither case has reached a public resolution.
A goodwill AI grant to the same country where both disputes remain unsettled is not necessarily cynical, but it is a pairing a careful reader notices.
Meta has not published a per-grant amount, an application process, or a firm opening date beyond “2027,” so it isn’t yet possible to say how far $700,000 actually stretches across seven countries.
Neither the Kenyan privacy probe nor the content moderator case has a confirmed resolution date, so there’s no way to know whether either will be settled before the new grant programme even opens.

It is also unconfirmed whether any of the showcased projects from this week’s summit, including Nigeria’s DAWN AI Study and South Africa’s dpclVR, will be eligible for the new grant or are being funded through a separate channel entirely.
The first thing to watch is whether Meta publishes real application details before 2027, since a headline grant with no process attached is still just a headline.

The second is whether either Kenyan case against Meta moves toward resolution before then, because a public outcome in either one would say more about Meta’s actual relationship with the region than a $700,000 announcement ever will.

items.description: The Kenya-UK Health Alliance is seeking to reduce Kenya’s dependence on foreign pharmaceutical innovations and funding by prioritising local drug research, domestic health financing and workforce development in its next strategic plan.
content: The Kenya-UK Health Alliance is seeking to reduce Kenya’s dependence on foreign pharmaceutical innovations and funding by prioritising local drug research, domestic health financing and workforce development in its next strategic plan.

Principal Secretary for Medical Services Dr Ouma Oluga said the partnership must shift towards building local capacity to develop medicines and health technologies while strengthening the country’s ability to finance its healthcare needs.

Speaking during a strategic planning seminar in Machakos County marking five years of the bilateral partnership, Oluga identified changing disease patterns, evolving health financing models and rising public expectations as key challenges shaping healthcare systems.
He called for increased investment in pharmaceutical research, drug development and the discovery of new molecules to reduce reliance on external innovations and patents.

The PS also emphasised the need to strengthen Primary Health Care to improve early detection and management of non-communicable diseases, including diabetes, hypertension, cardiovascular diseases, cancer and mental health conditions.
He noted that healthcare systems must also improve their preparedness for emerging public health threats linked to climate change, migration and human-animal interactions.
Oluga called for greater domestic resource mobilisation through the Social Health Authority (SHA), particularly as global donor priorities continue to change.

He said strengthening local financing mechanisms, investing in the health workforce, manufacturing health products locally and digitising healthcare services would be critical to building a sustainable health system.
The PS further urged health institutions, county governments and academic institutions to improve coordination and avoid duplication of investments in service delivery.
As the partnership enters its next phase, Oluga called for greater collaboration between institutions in Kenya and the UK through specialised training, professional exchanges and joint innovation.
He also urged partners to integrate research into routine clinical practice to ensure that scientific findings translate into better patient outcomes.

The five-year partnership brings together Kenyan and UK health institutions, academic bodies and other sector stakeholders to strengthen healthcare systems through institutional collaboration and knowledge exchange.
